# How Veles got its accent back

The ASCII form *veles* is missing something. **Veles** restores the ​marks the source language used to distinguish this name from a thousand others — and those marks change how the name is read, pronounced, and understood. This post explains, with the full ‌scholarly record behind it, what each restored mark preserves: the Slavic transcription evidence, the reconstructed sound, the myths the name carries, and the mechanical logic of what each restored mark preserves. By ‌the end, the marks in Veles will look less like ornaments and more like what they are — recovered evidence, pinned back in its proper place.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Veles
- ​**ASCII form:** veles
- **Meaning:** "Cattle god, possibly wool"
- **Domain of influence:** Cattle, Commerce, Underworld
- **Pantheon:** Slavic
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form

## Overview

**Veles** (*veles*) — Cattle, Commerce, Underworld · Cattle god, possibly wool — ​belongs to the Slavic tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Cattle, Commerce, Underworld". The name means "Cattle god, possibly wool".

**Veles** is cattle, commerce, underworld. The name means "Cattle god, ​possibly wool" and belongs to the slavic tradition.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Veles** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/veles/). The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form ​would lose. The plain ASCII form *veles* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## ​The Name

No indigenous written attestation survives for this name; **Veles** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means "Cattle god, possibly wool".

The ASCII form *veles* ‌survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Veles** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly ​transliteration directly in the address bar. ## Mythology

The stories of Veles place cattle, commerce, underworld at the center ​of a living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

Veles appears in slavic tradition as cattle, commerce, underworld. The name's meaning, "Cattle god, possibly wool", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and ​Memory (Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Veles in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of Veles survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. ​Each version reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare ​them. The restoration Veles gives the figure a stable name around which these variants orbit.

### Sworn by Volos (Oath-text)

The Rus'-Byzantine treaty of 944, copied into the Primary Chronicle, has left the ​only verbatim ritual text of pre-Christian Rus'. For the clauses of war the envoys swear by Perun; for everything touching livestock — sale, theft, compensation — they swear by Volos alone, and ‌the curse on the perjurer is total: 'may we be cursed by the god in whom we believe, by Perun and Volos, the furred one... may we not be protected by our ​shields, may we be slain by our own swords, may we be shot by our own arrows.' A later copyist glossed the unfamiliar name for his readers: 'Volos — that is, the ‌cattle god.' The division of labor is the myth in miniature: the sky-god witnesses between warriors, while the god of herds and wealth underwrites the peasant's entire fortune, animal by animal. Where ​your property lives, there your god is invoked.

### The Angry God of Suzdal (The Famine)

In the terrible famine year of 1024, the Primary Chronicle (s.a. 6532) tells how wandering sorcerers came ‌to Suzdal' and announced the cause of the people's misery: 'It is the god Veles who is angry.' The *volkhvy* demanded the sacrifice of a youth — a red-haired one, they specified, ​from a particular kin — and when the killing was done, they ate the body. The bishop of Rostov rode in, arrested the sorcerers, and drowned them in the Volga. The tale ‌is told by Christian enemies, and its details are horrific precisely in order to damn the old religion; yet its center is precious evidence. A generation after the baptism, when the official ​gods were Perun's rivals long drowned, it was still **Veles** whose name a prophet reached for when the earth would not feed her children. The underworld god was the one who explained ‌hunger.

### The Theft of the Cattle (Reconstruction)

In the reconstruction of Ivanov and Toporov, Slavic mythology's central cycle runs like this: Veles, dwelling in the underworld beneath the world-tree, commits a crime ​against the sky — he steals Perun's cattle, his treasure, sometimes his bride. Perun descends in pursuit, hurling his bolts; Veles transforms and wriggles — serpent, catfish, black eel — and each ​spring the thunderer strikes him down, and the rain returns to the herds. No East Slavic manuscript tells this story; it survives in the pairing of the gods in the treaty oaths, ‌in wedding laments where the bride weeps for a brother struck or drowned, in South Slavic spring songs, and in the universal Indo-European pattern of the storm-god and the serpent. The scholars ‌who built it were explicit that they were reconstructing — and the pieces fit with a stubbornness no rival hypothesis has matched.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Veles concentrates in ‌a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Name** — The restored form Veles, carrying scholarly and cultural weight.
- **Domain** — Cattle, Commerce, Underworld

Symbols function as a ​visual shorthand: they allow devotees and artists to recognize Veles across media and centuries. The attributes listed above are not decorative; each one encodes a claim about power, identity, or function. The ​restored spelling Veles carries the same precision in textual form.

- **Cattle horns** — The herds that were his treasure and the sign under which herders and merchants swore
- **The serpent** — His ‌disguise in the myth-cycle: low, wet, and close to the earth — the eternal adversary of the eagle
- **The bear** — His chthonic animal in the alternating lore of the Slavic year ​— master of the wilderness beyond the fence
- **Gusli (harp)** — The instrument of the singer he protects; in folklore the magic fiddle makes even the forest dance
- **Wet earth and roots** ​— The moist underworld into which he withdraws and from which wealth returns

## Archaeology & Evidence

No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is yet assigned to Veles with ‌certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Slavic name of this type the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the textual testimony gathered in ​the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming Veles, sanctuary or cult remains tied to cattle and iconography matching its traditional ​attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would be weighed against the reconstructed form of the name before entering the scholarly record.

## Realm & Domain

**Veles** is cattle, commerce, underworld. The name means ‌"Cattle god, possibly wool" and belongs to the slavic tradition.

### Sacred Name

The restoration Veles returns the figure to scholarly recognition.

### Cattle

### Living Tradition

Honored in slavic ​myth, cult, and cultural memory.

### Unicode Restoration

Preserved as a flagship temple despite the unregistrable plain-ASCII form.

### Lord of Cattle

The chronicles gloss him explicitly: Volos, 'the cattle god' — herders swore ‌their oaths by him alone.

### The Underworld River

He rules the wet, root-filled depths beneath the world-tree: the realm of the dead and of hidden treasure.

### God of Poetry

In the reconstructed ​mythology he is patron of singers and sorcerers; the wandering volkhvy acted in his name.

### Adversary of Perun

The eternal enemy in the myth-cycle: thief of cattle, storm of wealth, struck down ​each spring by the thunderer's bolt.

## A Meditation

To contemplate Veles is to hold the idea of cattle, Commerce, Underworld in the mind and to ask what of it ​endures. The name means "Cattle god, possibly wool" — and a name that carries its meaning so openly invites meditation rather than mere recollection. The tradition remembers the name as cattle, Commerce, ​Underworld · Cattle god, possibly wool.

Sit with the restored form — Veles — and the diacritics themselves become the practice: each mark is a small act of attention, a refusal to ‌let the plain ASCII form *veles* stand in for the whole. What the tradition preserved in this name, the restoration asks the reader to preserve in turn.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small ‌map. In the case of **Veles**, the map does not lead through diacritics or special letters, because the source tradition wrote the name in Slavic transcription rather than in the Latin alphabet. ​The ASCII form *veles* and the restored form share the same letters; the restoration is a decision about which conventional spelling should serve as the public reference.

That decision is not cosmetic. ‌The original script attestation carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization can fully reproduce. By fixing one conventional spelling as the canonical domain form, the project prevents the drift that happens ​when a name is romanized differently in every article, map, and database. The breakdown still lists each character — **v**, **e**, **l**, **e**, **s** — so visitors can see exactly what is ‌being carried forward and what is not. What looks like "no change" is, in fact, a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, and addressable.

The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way of keeping the name in the company of its kin. When the ‌address bar shows **Veles**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living catalog of myth. That catalog is the point of the project. Every ​restored name is a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, between a tradition and a trend. **Veles** is one such vote.
